passage: Arohi, you are still cross about Miss Fernandes, so listen to an old man. I am Kamal, your Nana. When I was ten, my teacher made me stand outside the class for a joke I had not made. I did not talk to her for a month. Then one day she stopped me in the corridor and said, "I was wrong to blame you. I am sorry." My eyes filled. I felt relief, but also a sore spot inside, like a scrape that had not healed. I nodded. Slowly I understood that teachers are people who slip too. When I forgave her, that weight left my chest.

qa.q: Where did the teacher make Kamal stand?
qa.a: She made him stand outside the class.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when his teacher apologised?
qa.a: He felt relieved but also still sore, like a scrape that had not healed.

qa.q: What might Arohi learn from Nana's story about her own anger at Miss Fernandes?
qa.a: She can accept a sincere apology and let herself forgive gently, without pretending it did not hurt, so she does not carry the anger. 🤍

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when she went up to Kamal in the corridor?
qa.a: She was probably uneasy and remorseful, since she had to admit her mistake to a child, and it took courage.

grounding: An elder recalls his teacher admitting she was wrong; he felt relief and a lingering ache, and forgiving gently lifted the anger.
